newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian ruling party claims legitimacy from vote.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian ruling party claims legitimacy from vote.

text.p: Indonesia's Golkar party said on Sunday its record victory in last week's election and the high turnout legitimised its rule, despite the most violent campaign ever.

Golkar General Chairman Harmoko, who is also information minister, said the turnout was around 90 percent of the country's 125 million registered voters. Golkar won a record 74.3 percent, compared with 68.1 percent in 1992 and its previous peak of 73.2 percent in 1987.

"This is proof that the people of Indonesia agree with the existing political and electoral systems, besides being a big legitimisation for (President Suharto's) New Order government," Harmoko said in a statement to a news conference.
Some diplomats questioned whether the overall vote in a carefully controlled political system could be regarded as a direct endorsement of Suharto and his policies.

But they said the size of the Golkar poll would make it easier for the 75-year-old president to seek a seventh five-year term of office next March, as widely expected. The president is elected and his policies endorsed in an assembly made up of the 500 members of parliament and 500 appointees.
Suharto's succession is a major issue for Indonesians and foreign investors, and there is much speculation about who his running mate will be.

Golkar's share of the vote far exceeded the 22.6 percent received by the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) and the 3.05 percent won by the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), which suffered a disastrous party split.
Harmoko dismissed suggestions that the more than 300 killings in the month preceding the vote were sign of frustration with the government and system.
"The violence which has happened in a number of areas is not political behaviour but criminal actions. We must differentiate," Harmoko said in response to questioning.
Political analysts have blamed a series of riots triggered by relatively minor incidents on poverty, frustration with the autocratic system of government and corruption.

Harmoko also rejected claims that there were systematic violations of electoral laws and vote rigging in favour of Golkar, as charged by an independent election watchdog set up activists and government critics.
The PPP also said there had been election irregularities and it would meet this week to decide whether to accept the result.
Local officials in East Java said they would conduct a re-vote on Madura island, near Indonesia's second city Surabaya, this week after angry crowds destroyed ballot boxes on Thursday.
Thousands of supporters of the PPP rioted, burning houses, offices and a church, alleging vote-rigging when Golkar appeared to be sweeping the election on the strongly-Moslem island.
